title: Bolded list-item header with explanation
description: This latent fires on sentences that begin with a short bolded phrase functioning as a list-item label or heading, followed by a colon and an explanatory sentence elaborating on that label. The included sentences are structured as 'Bolded Term**: explanation continues...', typically found in enumerated lists describing categories, traits, or features (e.g., job types, characteristics, options). It is not simply about topical content like jobs or schedules; the defining feature is the formatting pattern of a bolded label introducing a descriptive clause, not plain prose sentences discussing the same subject without this list-header structure.

title: Implementation intention instruction
description: This latent fires on bolded step headers that introduce the advice-list technique of forming an 'implementation intention'—i.e., specifying the concrete when/where/how details for executing a planned task. Included sentences are near-identical templated instructions that name the strategy and then direct the reader to define specific timing and location details for carrying it out. It is not about general goal-setting, motivation, or productivity tips broadly; it specifically captures this named cognitive-behavioral technique framed as a discrete, labeled action step within a list. Sentences discussing planning in other terms, or without the 'implementation intention' label and its when/where specification, are excluded.

title: Affirming self-worth and encouraging self-prioritization
description: This latent fires on formulaic, therapeutic-style affirmations that directly address the reader ('you') and validate their worth, strength, and right to prioritize their own well-being -- typically in the context of advice about relationships, breakups, abuse, or emotional healing. The highest-activating examples are near-identical templated phrases like 'You are strong, capable, and deserving of love and respect,' 'Remember, you deserve to be happy and fulfilled,' or 'You deserve to prioritize your own healing and well-being,' often beginning with 'Remember,' 'You are,' or 'You deserve.' Lower-activating cluster members are more varied advice-giving or reflective statements (e.g., self-care tips, bulleted action items, empathetic observations) that share the therapeutic/self-help register but lack the direct, formulaic affirmation-of-worth structure. Explicitly excluded are general advice, practical suggestions, questions for reflection, or third-person statements about other people's feelings/situations that don't directly affirm the reader's inherent worth or deservingness.

title: Naming an observed behavioral pattern
description: This latent fires on sentences where the speaker calls out a recurring, noticed pattern in another person's behavior, often as a lead-in to raising a concern or grievance (e.g., 'I've noticed that when you X, you usually Y'). Included sentences use first-person observational framing ('I've noticed', 'I've realized') paired with a habitual or repeated action described in general/present tense rather than a single one-off event. It does not include simple complaints without the noticing frame, isolated single-instance anecdotes, or statements that merely describe someone's trait without linking it to an observed recurring pattern of interaction.

title: List-item markers introducing advice steps
description: This latent fires on the structural tokens that introduce enumerated advice or suggestion lists -- bare numerals like '2.' or '3.', list-starting words like 'Consider', 'By', or 'By communicating', rather than on any topical content. The top-activating examples are almost purely these skeletal markers (numbered bullet openers, transition words that begin a clause explaining a method), which typically precede advice about communication, relationships, or conflict resolution in an assistant-style response. The random cluster examples show the fuller sentences these markers introduce (e.g., relationship advice, conversation tips), but the latent's core trigger is the enumerating/structuring token itself, not the semantic content of the advice. It is NOT capturing the topic of interpersonal communication per se -- sentences about communication that lack this list-initiating or enumerative structure would not activate it as strongly.

title: Numbered list item markers
description: This latent fires on the numeral (and often trailing period or bold-markdown asterisks) that begins an item in an enumerated list, such as '3.', '4. **', or '9.'. The activating token is essentially just the list-numbering marker itself, largely independent of the actual content or topic of the list (advice, pros/cons, tips, steps, etc.). It captures the structural/formatting role of marking sequential list items rather than any semantic content of the sentence. It does NOT capture the substantive text of list items themselves (e.g., 'Find affordable food options' or 'Get comfortable with your vehicle') except insofar as they immediately follow or contain such a numeral marker; sentences without a numbered/bulleted list structure, or full prose without enumeration markers, are excluded.

title: Empathetic exclamatory framing openers
description: This latent fires on short, formulaic exclamatory or greeting phrases that an assistant (often in an advice-giving or Reddit-AITA-style context) uses to preface or frame its response emotionally, before delivering actual substance. It includes stock exclamations like 'The age-old dilemma!', 'What a tricky situation!', 'The drama!', empathetic openers like 'I totally get it!' and 'I completely understand!', and greetings like 'Hello there!'—all functioning as tone-setting or rapport-building interjections rather than content. It does NOT include the actual advice, tips, verdicts (e.g., 'NTA', 'you're not the asshole'), or substantive reasoning that follows these openers, nor does it include longer explanatory or list-formatted content even when topically similar.

title: Verdict statements on someone's behavior (AITA-style judgment)
description: This latent fires on short, declarative verdict sentences that assign moral judgment to a specific party's reaction or behavior in an interpersonal-conflict narrative, typically of the form '[Person]'s [reaction/behavior] was [unacceptable/unreasonable/unfair/entitled/etc.]'. The highest-activating examples are terse, standalone judgment sentences (often list-numbered) that directly label a person's conduct as wrong, excessive, or problematic, frequently using a bare possessive subject ('Your mom's reaction was...', 'D's behavior was...') plus a negative evaluative predicate, and also fires on isolated list-marker numerals (2., 3., 4.) that structurally precede these verdicts. It is NOT simply about discussing interpersonal conflict or advice-column content in general—longer explanatory, hedged, or empathetic sentences that justify, contextualize, or soften a judgment (e.g., 'it's understandable that...', 'while I understand your frustration...') activate much more weakly and belong to the random/background sample rather than the core pattern, which specifically targets crisp, unqualified condemnatory verdicts.
